assertion_3_wrong_role_boundary_and_core.the_proof: In certification-result.md the referent of 'that signature' is the immediately preceding clause: 'false positives exceed false negatives by 637 arguments (4,434 against 3,797), which is systematic over-generation'. There is no other candidate antecedent in the blockquote. But `fp - fn = prediction_count - gold_count`, so an error that REPLACES one predicted argument with another cannot change fp - fn by even one. A wrong-role error emits the same argument under a different role: one fp, one fn, net zero. A boundary/normalization mismatch emits the same argument with different offsets: one fp, one fn, net zero. A coreference/alias mismatch emits a different string for the same slot: one fp, one fn, net zero. All three are substitutions, and NO substitution can contribute to a 637-argument excess. The categories that can are section 12.1's 'extra grounded but incorrect argument' and 'duplicate argument' — neither of which the sentence names.

R3_the_section_11_1_redisposition.why_the_ground_is_unsound: The descope reason given is 'the section 8.5 ground that re-defining the document loss after seeing an infeasible result is a post-hoc re-score'. Section 8.5 does not reach this item, on two independent grounds, both readable in the plan's primary text. FIRST, nothing is being RE-defined: section 4.1 PREDECLARES this analysis — 'The strict sensitivity analysis uses maximum frame loss per document. It does not replace the primary result because it looks stronger or weaker.' The plan already anticipated the exact concern the disposition raises and already answered it, before any result was seen. Running a predeclared sensitivity is not a post-hoc re-score; it is the plan. SECOND, section 8.5 forbids RESCUING A FAILED HYPOTHESIS, and its own carve-out says such analyses 'may appear as labelled exploratory work if predeclared and multiplicity-aware, but they cannot change the primary conclusion'. Maximum frame loss is >= mean frame loss on every multi-frame group, so it is a STRICTLY HARSHER loss: it can only make the null more emphatic. An analysis that cannot move the result toward feasibility cannot be a rescue, and section 8.5's carve-out permits it by name.
R3_the_section_11_1_redisposition.why_this_matters_rather_than_being_pedan: The document's own opening states the defect it exists to repair: 'The defect is not that items were skipped. It is that mootness was assumed rather than ruled.' A descope on a rule the plan text contradicts is that defect in a third costume — first 'executed' when it was not run, now 'descoped under section 8.5' when section 8.5 expressly permits it. It is also the only row in the table whose stated ground the plan contradicts: the section 8.5 citations on the two NEIGHBOURING rows are both apt (normalized span matching is a LOOSER criterion, which could rescue; completion-mean-NLL is 'switching to a secondary score', which section 8.5 lists verbatim). q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.verdict: CORRECT, AND SAFE IN THIS REPOSITORY — verified empirically over the whole corpus rather than argued. Two narrow residual gaps, both false-NEGATIVE only, neither live today.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.the_change: tests/test_withdrawn_assertions.py::_flat went from `' '.join(text.split())` to stripping a leading '>' from every line before collapsing whitespace: `[line.lstrip().removeprefix('>').lstrip() for line in text.splitlines()]`.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.why_it_was_needed: The register's stale-exemption guard (test_every_exemption_still_earns_its_place) asserts every permitted_in file still contains its phrase. docs/plan3/certification-result.md quotes the withdrawn appositive inside a dated '>' blockquote, wrapped across two lines, so the phrase acquired a '>' in the middle and stopped matching — and the exemption was rejected as stale on a file that legitimately carried the phrase. The diagnosis in the commit message is exactly right and the class it names is real: this repository records every correction as a dated blockquote quoting the withdrawn wording, so the miss lands precisely in the documents most likely to carry a retired assertion legitimately.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.empirical_safety_test_i_ran: For all three register entries against every tracked file with a prose suffix, I computed the match under the OLD _flat and under the NEW _flat and printed every file whose status CHANGED. Exactly ONE changed: docs/plan3/certification-result.md, for entry grounding-orthogonal-coref-entity-selection, old=False new=True, and that file IS in permitted_in. So the normalisation flipped precisely the intended file and precisely the intended direction, and introduced NO new offender and NO new exemption anywhere else in the repository.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.false_positive_analysis: The theoretical false positive is a needle that spans a boundary the '>' used to break — i.e. text before a blockquote joining to text inside it to spell a registered phrase. It cannot arise from stripping alone, because the old _flat already joined all lines with a space; stripping only DELETES a token from that stream, so it can only create a match where a '>' previously interrupted one. For a false positive you would need prose ending in the phrase's prefix immediately followed by a blockquote beginning with its suffix. The empirical sweep found none, and the construction is implausible for phrases of this length. No false positive.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.false_negative_gap_1_nested_blockquotes: removeprefix('>') strips ONE marker. A nested line '> > text' becomes '> text' and would still break a match. `git grep -n '^\s*>\s*>' -- '*.md'` returns nothing, so no nested blockquote exists in this repository today. A future one would silently reopen the exact miss this fix closed. Cheap fix if wanted: strip repeatedly rather than once. Nit N7.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.false_negative_gap_2_blockquotes_inside_: PROSE_SUFFIXES includes .json, and reviewer records routinely embed multi-line markdown inside string values. In raw JSON a newline inside a string is the two-character escape \n, so the file has one physical line and _flat's per-line strip never fires — an embedded '>' marker survives into the flattened text and can break a match. This is not hypothetical in kind (the records quote blockquoted corrections verbatim), though I found no live instance. Nit N7.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.a_third_observation_not_a_gap: lstrip() before removeprefix means an indented '>' is handled, which is correct for blockquotes nested in list items. And a bare '>' line flattens to empty and joins harmlessly. Both right.
q8_is_the_blockquote_normalisation_corre.the_docstring_is_honest_about_it: The new docstring records both misses that produced this function (line wraps, then blockquote markers) and says each was 'found by running this rather than reading it'. That is the right register and it is the second time in this file's short life that running the check taught something reading it did not.

the_item_i_was_asked_to_attack_hardest.method: I did not read the four companions and judge them. For each I identified the exact set the GATE iterates, the exact set the COMPANION bounds, and then measured both, so that 'bounds the scanned set' versus 'bounds something adjacent' is a number rather than an opinion. I then asked, for each, what a silent collapse would look like and whether the companion survives it.

companion_1_test_the_register_is_populat.gate_it_guards: test_a_withdrawn_assertion_survives_only_where_named, which iterates `_prose_files()`; and the parametrisation over `_register()`, which would silently collapse to a single skipped test if the register emptied.
companion_1_test_the_register_is_populat.does_it_bound_the_scanned_set: YES on cardinality. `assert len(_prose_files()) > 50` calls the SAME nullary function the gate iterates — not a re-derivation, the same object. `assert _register()` bounds the other collapse route. Both dimensions that can go empty are covered.
companion_1_test_the_register_is_populat.BUT_it_does_not_bound_the_property_that_: MEASURED: under the reverted `git ls-files` implementation, `_prose_files()` returns 202 files. `len(...) > 50` passes. So if anyone reverted the walk to the index — which IS the B2 defect, exactly — this companion would be green, the gate would be blind to untracked files again, and nothing in the module would notice. The guard bounds CARDINALITY; B2 was a failure of SCOPE KIND, and the two are independent.
companion_1_test_the_register_is_populat.the_asymmetry_that_makes_this_sharp: tests/test_internal_paths.py HAS the missing test: `test_the_scan_reaches_untracked_files` writes a probe file, asserts the scanner sees it, and removes it — and its docstring says in terms 'If this ever passes trivially the scanner has quietly become index-based and the whole test is theatre.' tests/test_withdrawn_assertions.py has no equivalent. The fix inherited the IMPLEMENTATION from the module that learned the lesson and did not inherit the TEST that proves the implementation is of the right kind. That is the exact 'second half' the same commit wrote down — a hard-won scope decision living in one check's implementation gets rediscovered the expensive way — recurring one level up, at the test of the scope decision, in the commit that recorded the lesson.
companion_1_test_the_register_is_populat.ruling: WEAKER THAN CLAIMED. Sound as a cardinality guard; silent on the property whose failure produced the rule.

symlinks.finding: A genuine blind spot, and NOT a regression. Python is 3.12.13 here; `pathlib.Path.rglob` has signature `(self, pattern, *, case_sensitive=None)` — no `recurse_symlinks` parameter, and `**` does not descend into symlinked directories. A symlinked documentation tree would be invisible to both scanners. `git ls-files` had the same blind spot from the other direction (git records the link, not the target), so nothing was lost in the rewrite.

attack_1_is_30_the_right_bound_for_scann.verdict: NO. It is too loose by a wide margin, AND a bound is the wrong instrument for the failure it is being asked to detect. But the companion is not worthless, because the assertion beside the number is doing the real work. Required item E3.

the_measurements.corpus: `_scanned_markdown()` returns 63 files: 57 under `docs/`, 6 at the root.
the_measurements.headroom: The threshold is `> 30`, so the walk may lose 32 files — 51% of the corpus — and still pass.
the_measurements.every_single_subtree_can_drop_and_still_: I enumerated every top-two-level location and removed each in turn. Largest is `docs/plan2` at 13 files: dropping it leaves 50, passes. `docs/adr` leaves 51, passes. `docs/gate0` 54, `docs/plan3` 55, the entire root 57, `docs/plan4` 58 — all pass. There is NO single subtree whose loss the number detects. Not one.
the_measurements.what_the_number_does_catch: Only near-total collapse. `ROOT.glob('*.md')` instead of `rglob` yields 6 files and fails. That is the one mechanism the threshold is sized for.
the_measurements.what_the_number_does_not_catch_but_the_m: `(ROOT/'docs').rglob('*.md')` — the most plausible partial narrowing, a walk re-rooted at docs/ — yields 57 files and PASSES `> 30`. It is caught only by `assert 'README.md' in scanned`. So in the single realistic partial-collapse case the named-member assertion is the whole guard and the number contributes nothing.

attack_1_is_30_the_right_bound_for_scann.why_a_bound_is_structurally_the_wrong_in: A cardinality floor can only ever detect collapse toward zero. Any threshold below the true count tolerates narrowing down to that threshold; any threshold at the true count fails on every legitimate file addition or deletion, which produces churn and trains people to bump the number without looking — and that is the stale-count defect `tests/test_internal_paths.py`'s own docstring already rejects for the exemption list ('Carry an exclusion list, never a count. A bare count is stale the moment anything legitimately quotes one'). The repository has therefore already reasoned its way to the right conclusion in one place and built the opposite in another. Worth noticing: the guard-the-guard convention is entirely counts, and the exclusion-list convention forbids them. Both are right in their own domain; the tension is unnamed.
attack_1_is_30_the_right_bound_for_scann.the_instrument_that_does_work_and_is_alr: Cross-check the filesystem walk against the INDEX as a subset assertion, rather than choosing between them. MEASURED at HEAD: `git ls-files '*.md'` after the same skip conditions gives 63 files; `set(git_known) <= set(_scanned_markdown())` is TRUE and the walk has ZERO extras. A subset assertion is exact today, has no magic number, needs no maintenance when files are added or removed, is derived from a second source of truth rather than restating the first, and detects ANY narrowing of the walk relative to what git knows — including every subtree loss the `> 30` bound misses. It also composes with the kind probe rather than duplicating it: the probe catches the walk failing to see what the index cannot (untracked files); the subset catches the walk failing to see what the index can. Together they pin the set from both sides. The index-versus-filesystem distinction this repository learned the expensive way is more useful as a CROSS-CHECK than as a choice.
attack_1_is_30_the_right_bound_for_scann.what_i_recommend_concretely: Keep `assert 'README.md' in scanned` — it is the load-bearing half. Replace or supplement `> 30` with the subset cross-check. If a number is kept for the total-collapse case, size it against the corpus rather than at half of it, and say in the docstring that it detects collapse and not narrowing, which is the same honesty the sibling docstring now shows about cardinality versus kind.
attack_1_is_30_the_right_bound_for_scann.the_same_criticism_applies_to_the_other_: `> 50` on `_prose_files()` against 202 actual, `> 50` on `_known_identifiers()`, `> 20` on `_referenced_identifiers()` against 45 actual — all have the same structural limit. I do not raise them as required items because (a) `tests/test_internal_paths.py` and `tests/test_withdrawn_assertions.py` both carry a kind probe, which is the guard that actually matters for them, and (b) `test_doc_references.py`'s `> 20` I already measured as catching its realistic collapse. attack_2_does_scanned_markdown_need_a_ki.the_rule_as_written: 'Every scanning gate needs the cardinality guard; a gate whose scope was itself the defect needs the kind probe too.'
attack_2_does_scanned_markdown_need_a_ki.why_that_clause_is_a_loophole: `_scanned_markdown()`'s scope was never the defect — it has always been an rglob — so by the letter of the rule it is exempt. question_1_does_the_cross_check_cover_th.why_it_fails_analytically: The cross-check makes two assertions: (a) `tracked ⊆ scanned` — no tracked markdown is missed; (b) `(scanned − tracked) ∩ gitignored = ∅` — nothing gitignored is included. question_3_is_the_self_critical_overstat.the_rule_as_written: 'Overstatement in the self-critical direction is still overstatement, and nothing checks it because it reads as humility.' But a retraction that goes further than the data destroys a sound rule, and the cost lands on whoever needed that rule later.'
question_3_is_the_self_critical_overstat.overstatement_a_nothing_checks_it_is_ref: Something did check it: an independent reviewer, in this sequence, which is the only reason the instance exists to be written up. 'Nothing checks it' is a universal that the existence of its own instance falsifies. The accurate form is narrower and still forceful: no AUTOMATED check sees it, and a reviewer is unlikely to challenge it, because challenging a concession looks like defending the party who made it. Note the shape — this is an overstatement of how exposed the process is, i.e. an overstatement in the self-critical direction, inside the rule about overstatement in the self-critical direction. Third order, and cheap to fix.
question_3_is_the_self_critical_overstat.overstatement_b_destroys_is_false_of_the: 'A retraction that goes further than the data destroys a sound rule.' This new rule has ONE instance and is written as a rule. The defensible answer is that it comes with a stated MECHANISM — nobody audits a concession, the party it costs is the party making it — and a mechanism plus one instance is a stronger basis than an instance count. But the document does not say that, and it applied the stricter standard one bullet earlier, so as it stands the repository holds two different bars for the same promotion with nothing distinguishing them.
question_3_is_the_self_critical_overstat.what_is_right_about_it_and_should_not_be: The core observation is correct, non-obvious and genuinely transferable: the reason a self-critical overstatement survives is structural, not psychological — the only party with standing to object is the party it flatters to leave standing. And the prescription is the best sentence in the bullet: 'Concede exactly as much as the evidence requires, and no more — then say which part survives, in the same breath.' F1_scanned_markdown_violates_the_univers.file: tests/test_gate_state.py, and REVIEW.md's operative kind-guard rule
F1_scanned_markdown_violates_the_univers.what_is_wrong: REVIEW.md states in bold, in the operative bullet: 'Every gate that walks the filesystem needs the kind guard', and 'A rule that exempts a gate until it has already failed is not a rule.' `_scanned_markdown()` walks the filesystem and has no kind guard. The stated reason — that the index cross-check covers both directions so a probe adds nothing — is false, and analytically so: an index-based walk returns exactly `tracked`, which makes `tracked ⊆ scanned` a tautology and `scanned − tracked` empty, so both halves of the cross-check pass BY CONSTRUCTION under the implementation the kind guard exists to reject. MEASURED with an untracked markdown file present: filesystem walk n=64, both assertions pass; `git ls-files` walk n=63, both assertions pass; the kind probe sees the file under the first and not the second. The violation is disclosed nowhere — the fourth exposure in docs/plan4/open-release-decisions.md discloses the over-inclusion gap in the OTHER two walks, which is a different guard.
F1_scanned_markdown_violates_the_univers.why_it_blocks: It is a normative universal in a gate document that the repository does not satisfy, undisclosed, introduced in the same commit that made the rule universal — the same class as the two coverage claims already blocked on in this sequence. In its docstring, record that the cross-check cannot substitute for it and why — that an index-based walk satisfies both cross-check assertions by construction — because that is the non-obvious part and it is what stops the argument being made again. If instead the exemption is kept, state it in REVIEW.md immediately beside the universal rule with the reason, so the rule is not stated wider than the repository satisfies; but the argument as it stands is measurably wrong and should not be the reason.
F1_scanned_markdown_violates_the_univers.explicitly_not_asked: Do not weaken the universal rule, and do not remove or weaken the cross-check. The cross-check closes two real holes the floor did not and I verified both. The finding is that it closes different holes from the ones a probe closes, not that it is the wrong instrument.
